topics.title: [grug] Compute the MoE routing-weight gradient on the expert side
topics.body:
The hero takes its MoE routing-weight gradient from the expert MLP's own backward, so the backward needs neither the expert outputs nor their return transport, and the hero saves the routed output instead of recomputing the expert down projection, the return all-to-all and the combine. The step shortens by 4.12% (13.541 to 13.005 s against #9832, over 26 scored steps). Peak HBM rises to 125.4 GiB of the 143.75 GiB pool.

`moe_mlp` and `MoEExpertMlp` gain `routing_weight_gradient`. The default, `EXACT`, keeps the expert outputs and differentiates the combine, as before. `EXPERT_SIDE` is the new path, which the hero selects; other implementations reject it. Where w * dout rounds to zero in the cotangent dtype (a zero weight, or in float16 a normal weight times a small cotangent), its gradient is zero or inexact. The hero's routing weights are positive renormalized sigmoids and its cotangents bf16, which has fp32's exponent range. Forward, dx, dW13 and dW2 are bitwise unchanged; the routing-weight gradient differs at bf16 rounding (median ~1 ulp) at nonzero weights.

The gradient with respect to the combine weight w[t,k] is dS[t,k] = <dout[t], y[t,k]>, the only backward consumer of the expert down projection's output y. Since dy = w * dout and dh = dy W2^T, the same value is rowsum(dh * h) / w, built from tensors the expert MLP backward already holds. One custom VJP from dispatch to combine returns s = <h, dh> per expert row, sends it back with one [C, 1] f32 all-to-all per chunk, and forms dS = s / w in f32; dropped and padded slots get 0 by selection. The portable `ragged_dot` expert MLP, used without QuACK, still keeps its outputs for the row dot. The backward's transports reuse the forward transfers' offsets, swapped, and on GPU its weighted output cotangents come from #9832's scatter kernel.

The saved routed output fits the 114 GiB remat budget that #9831 gives the carry offload; the backward needs ~105 GiB. With the backward's transports no longer ordered after the recompute's, several collectives in flight gave run-to-run different gradients or hung on GB200, so every ragged run forces a collective overlap limit of 1.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0), each head compiled fresh.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [levanter] Replace the Pallas short convolution with a Triton kernel
topics.body:
Short convolutions on GPU run in a new streaming Triton kernel that reads each tensor once, instead of once per tap. The Pallas kernel is deleted, and the package moves from `levanter.kernels.pallas.short_conv` to `levanter.kernels.triton.short_conv`. In a single-GPU hero block, short-convolution time per step falls from 4.45 to 1.76 ms.

| Shape | Direction | Previous Pallas | Triton |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | forward | 423.9 us | 226.4 us |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | backward | 1024.3 us | 380.7 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | forward | 103.2 us | 59.3 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | backward | 262.9 us | 105.3 us |

Median kernel time per call on one GB200, 9 documents per sequence. The forward runs at the HBM floor of a read-one-write-one stream on the same tensor, and the backward at 1.14 times its floor. A port of the same algorithm to Pallas reached 230.0 and 403.7 us at C=6144, and needed code-generation workarounds (an inline-asm FMA, program ids clamped to the grid) that steer XLA's Triton pipeline.

The kernel takes kernel size 4, a channel count that is a multiple of 64, and bfloat16 or float32. The wrapper right-pads each local sequence to a multiple of 128 rows with the out-of-range segment id and drops the padded outputs, so any sequence length runs on the kernel. Other calls fall back to `short_conv_reference` with a warning. Every caller gets the kernel, so `GrugModelConfig.sconv_implementation` is removed; checkpoints are unchanged.

The forward and dx are bit-identical to `short_conv_reference` in bfloat16 and float32; dw changes only in fp32 summation order. On SM90 and newer the bf16 multiplies and adds are packed PTX (`mul.rn.bf16x2`, `add.rn.bf16x2`). Older GPUs take an fp32 op and a bf16 cast, which rounds the same way, and Triton's fp fusion is off so that LLVM cannot contract that fallback into a bf16 FMA that rounds once. The fallback has run on GB200 with the capability check forced, but not on an SM80 GPU.

Each program walks a sequence chunk of one channel block. It carries the previous three rows of x (in the backward also the next three rows of dy) and their segment ids in registers, and loads every row of a step before storing any; the backward writes one fp32 dw partial per chunk. A step whose rows lie in one document skips the segment masks, which cuts a backward step from 467 to 275 SASS instructions.

No rack run measured this kernel alone. On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), an earlier version that was 7-15% slower per call shortened the step by 0.55%.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [grug] Keep hero eval and FLOPs metrics continuous across a relaunch
topics.body:
GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len fixes the held-out eval context independently of the training context, so a run that changes context can keep scoring at 4K and its eval_dropless/* series stays comparable. The first-step eval now also runs after a checkpoint resume, once, so each relaunch checks the eval-to-train handoff immediately instead of at the next periodic eval. The dropless eval reports evaluation start and end progress events, as the other evals do.

Per-example FLOPs rise with context length, so the cumulative throughput/total_gflops would jump at a context switch. A FlopsBaseline (completed steps and cumulative FLOPs at the handoff) adds the parent's history to the new shape's count; current MFU uses the new attention cost. run_progress now divides by the full schedule length when stop_after_steps bounds a run, so a bounded diagnostic reports the same progress as the full run at the same step.

Stacked on #9888. Part of #9615

- **What it does.** `ring` all-gathers every token to all 8 GPUs and reduce-scatters a full-size output, but with top-4 of 256 experts a token reaches only 3.3 GPUs on average. `ring_dedup` (new module `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring_dedup.py`) sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`, plus a small `all_to_all` of per-row combine weights and local expert ids. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule, grouped layout and Triton `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32 and returns one row per token. All hidden-width movement is a gather (ring's `_dispatch_rows`/`_combine_rows`), so there are no scatter-adds in either pass.
- **Sender capacity** is `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing (0.416 × 32,768 per GPU). At 1.1 it sends 537 MB per collective per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring's all-gather or reduce-scatter (46%), and drops no tokens at the sender in these runs.
- **A/B, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile cache per job, `JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`, median of steps 2-19:**

  | merged | save_moe | 1.730 s, 13.07% | 1.580 s, 14.31% (-8.7%) | 454012, 454021 |
  | before the gather combine | recompute_all | 1.865 s, 12.13% | 1.735 s, 13.03% (-7.0%) | 453921, 453922 |
  | before the gather combine | save_moe | 1.842 s, 12.28% | 1.637 s, 13.81% (-11.1%) | 453960, 453968 |

Step-19 loss is within 8e-4 of ring in every pair. The drop rate is 1.00% vs 0.99% (`recompute_all`) and 1.12% vs 0.93% (`save_moe`).
- **Numerics.** f32 CPU unit tests on 8 shards match ring and a dense reference to 1e-5 in value and in gradients for x, combine weights and both expert weights, including a forced sender-drop case. At full shapes in bf16 on MI350X, one layer differs from ring by 0.2-0.5% relative in value and gradients. That comes from ring's bf16 summation; `ring_dedup` sums in f32.

Each large `all_to_all` takes 1.6-2.7 ms, against 3.3-4.2 ms for ring's collectives.

Since diagnosed as allocator fragmentation around the step's temp buffer and fixed by `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` (#9901).
- **Follow-ups:** packing the metadata into the activation rows and chunking the expert MLP were tried and did not help; see the next comment. Not tested on TPU or NVIDIA.

### One gradient all-reduce per weight after the layer scan: works, keeps gradients, no speedup on MI350X

| 60b253d | recompute_all | deferred reduction | 1.852 s | 141,600 | 12.21% | 158.4 GiB |

| 67ca557 | recompute_all | baseline | 1.786 s | 146,800 | 12.66% | 157.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | recompute_all | deferred reduction | 1.786 s | 146,800 | 12.66% | 157.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | save_moe | baseline | 1.748 s | 150,000 | 12.94% | 205.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | save_moe | deferred reduction | 1.741 s | 150,600 | 12.99% | 205.9 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- What the in-scan all-reduces are: on this mesh (`expert=8`, other axes 1), every non-expert block weight is replicated across the batch. Explicit sharding types each layer's weight gradient as replicated, so the backward while body all-reduces it per layer. Per layer that is 5 gradient all-reduces: q/k/v/gate and w_o in the attention `cond` branch, one combined GatedNorm/router/shared w_gate/w_up, shared w_down, and the two RMSNorm weights. The forward body adds one router-stats all-reduce, for 6 × 26 = 156 per step. XLA's combiner can't merge across loop iterations or `cond` branches.
- The change: weights that only feed matmuls are marked `reduced` over the batch axes before the scan (`levanter.grug.sharding.defer_batch_grad_reduction`). Their gradients leave the scan unreduced and are all-reduced once per stacked weight. FSDP-sharded leaves (`data` > 1) are left unchanged. RMSNorm weights keep the per-layer reduction. Stored parameter shardings don't change.
- Gradients match. On CPU (tiny preset, f32, 8 devices) the loss and 26 of 27 leaves are bit-identical. On GPU (medium preset, bf16, job 454079) the loss is identical, and baseline-vs-change errors (at most 0.63% relative L2) equal baseline-vs-baseline. The full-model losses match too.
- The backward loop goes from 5 gradient all-reduces per layer to 1, but the step doesn't get faster. In a profiled A/B (job 453987) the change saves 43 ms per step, but the profiler adds about 0.3 ms to every collective call. Unprofiled, the 130 removed calls cost about 11 ms, and the single 2 GB all-reduce after the scan takes about 16 ms on the main stream. The bytes are the same either way, and the per-layer calls were bandwidth-bound, not latency-bound.
- Not proposing a PR for MI350X. Small collectives should be priced from unprofiled step times, not from trace durations.

</details>

topics.title: [levanter] Stop background iterators after completion
topics.body:
Buffered background iterators now remain stopped after the producer finishes or raises. Previously, consuming the single end marker or error left later `next()` calls waiting forever on an empty queue. Levanter uses this iterator to prefetch data loader batches and evaluation requests.

Regression tests reproduce the hang after normal exhaustion and producer failure in bounded and unbounded queues. The affected safe suite passed 1,063 tests with 13 skips.

topics.title: [grug] Add the H100 pipeline foundation
topics.body:
Add a stage-local JAXPP pipeline for the full MoE model blocks, including latent/shared experts, SConv, attention positions and QB routing. Standard 1F1B remains the default. The synthetic runner supports the main recipe with FP32 parameters, BF16 compute and compute-scaled MuonH; the historical BF16 capacity recipe remains available.

Each routed expert parameter bank now shares one Frobenius norm across its experts, matching the stacked EP model. `--expert-normalization per_expert` provides an explicit comparison mode. `--qb-bias-mode frozen` retains the current pending QB bias while expert and router weights continue updating; adaptive QB remains the default. Numerical CPU regressions cover stacked-versus-stage-local updates and both QB state transitions.

The historical 48-layer, 65K synthetic diagnostic ran on 192 H100s with BF16-stored parameters and per-expert normalization. Its PP24/EP8/CP1 layout placed two layers in each stage and kept expert traffic within eight-GPU workers. It was chosen to establish capacity; no matched PP8/EP32/CP4 Megatron comparison was performed. The README records the later CP2 result and the differences in batch size and attention helpers. Historical hardware results do not validate the new normalization or frozen-QB option, and no SFT/RL quality comparison has been run.

The affected safe suite passed 2,391 tests with four skips and five expected failures. Focused CPU checks passed 86 tests with one skip; required lint, full type checking, strict docs and source links passed.

#9662 is stacked above this foundation and adds checkpoint/data support, the GB200 launcher, tracked runtime setup and bounded main-recipe hardware validation. Before merge, this foundation still owns replacing the positional result from `initialize_stage_local_pipeline_state`, centralizing the repeated backend/rematerialization identifiers, and separating the synthetic runner lifecycle in `pipeline_smoke.main`. These deferred changes require compiled-startup transport and optimizer-parking/warmup cleanup validation; #9662 then owns adapting its added checkpoint/data lifecycle.

topics.title: [grug] Leave ragged MoE transport rows unwritten when nothing reads them
topics.body:
The ragged all-to-all MoE stops zero-filling and overwriting transport rows that no consumer reads, and on GPU builds its dispatch buffer with one scatter. Outputs, drops and gradients are bitwise unchanged. One MoE layer's forward and backward is 4.4-4.8% faster and its compiler temp 1.37 GB smaller, and the hero step shortens by 1.41% (13.732 to 13.541 s against #9831, over 26 scored steps).

The expert chunks write disjoint rows of the dispatch and return buffers, but the custom VJP around `ragged_all_to_all` differentiated each write as an overwrite, so every layer's backward spent a [TK, H] select, add and zero fill on rows the next chunk would ignore. Each written row holds nothing before its one write, and for such a row an overwrite has the derivative of an add, so the transpose passes the output cotangent through unchanged. With every consumer reading only rows a collective wrote, the buffers need no fill: on GPU they come from a Triton kernel that writes nothing, elsewhere they are zero-filled. Each buffer is tied to a loop-carried value, because XLA would otherwise hoist an input-free buffer out of the layer loop and copy it into every layer's output slot. Dropped and padded slots get combine weight 0, and the combine and dispatch-gradient sums skip them. A GPU test fills every buffer with NaN instead of zero and requires identical outputs, drop counts and gradients under 22 routings, among them an expert no token selects, a receiver chunk and a whole receiver with no rows, a sender with only padding, and near-total drops, with two chunks of three experts per GPU as on the hero.

On GPU, a Triton kernel builds the expert-sorted dispatch buffer by reading each token's row once and writing it to the token's accepted slots, where a gather read every row topk times: 0.535 ms (6.6 TB/s) at the hero's per-GPU routed shape (TK = 524288 rows of the 3072-wide latent). Its weighted form serves #9833's backward. The gather-sum's forward loops over 1024-wide hidden tiles, which keeps more programs resident: 0.508 ms against 0.574 ms.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0), each head compiled fresh.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [post-training] Compare SFT, rejection-sampled SFT and OPD transfer on Snowball with CruxEval
topics.body:
Design doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1LVfMDHRBKBk_Bn9PY1J9Lb_MYwdUTFP5PkX2br25TNg/edit?tab=t.izhzsywzorld (owner is updating it; this issue is the summary and coordination record).

**TL;DR.** Given one expert model E built from the Snowball student B, compare how much of E's gain each transfer method recovers and at what cost: SFT on E's traces, SFT on rejection-sampled E traces, and on-policy distillation (OPD) from E. Benchmark: CruxEval, training on the test prompts. Status: E is training; no arm has run yet.

**Models.** Student B = `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`. E = B after full SFT on GLM 5.3 traces (recipe from marin#9775: fresh AdamH state, frozen router biases). E keeps B's tokenizer and chat template. Every arm starts from B.

**Benchmark.** CruxEval (800 Python functions; input prediction and output prediction scored separately by executing the assertion). MATH500 was dropped because B already scores 89.8% there. Both CruxEval tasks are trained and reported separately.

**Teacher gate (done).** Under the frozen evaluator, B scores 55.4% input / 57.8% output. GLM 5.3 on the identical 1,600 prompts scores 94.0% / 90.5% (1,600/1,600 answered, none truncated). GLM also scores 84.4% on MMLU-Pro and 79.3% on GPQA-Diamond against B's prior 43.7 / 43.1, kept as fallback benchmarks.

**Frozen evaluator.** Marin `experiments.evaluation.cli launch` with Evalchemy `c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2`, vLLM on H100x8 (DP8 + EP8), `max_model_len` 32768, `max_gen_toks` 30720, `enable_thinking: true`, reasoning parser `grug`. Configs and pitfalls: https://gist.github.com/ksagar1030/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71. One correction found on the way: Evalchemy's chat client sends no temperature, top_p or seed, and B's `generation_config.json` sets none, so every run samples at vLLM's default (temperature 1.0, unseeded). Single-pass noise on 800 problems is about ±3.5 points; final candidates get two passes.

**Building E (in progress).** 1,454 GLM CruxEval traces that pass execution and carry reasoning (751 input, 703 output), rendered in B's native format: reasoning, then `<|end_think|>`, then the answer. 592k supervised tokens per epoch, longest row 22,835 tokens. First run: LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 273 updates, 32 H100s; exports after updates 92, 183 and 273. Other learning rates only if this run fails the gate. W&B: `marin-community/cruxeval-transfer-133`. Gate: E ≥ B + 10 points on both CruxEval tasks with no GSM8K drop beyond noise (B: 90.4).

**Arms (planned, all from B, matched prompt budget, same LR/epoch sweep for the SFT arms as for OPD).**
- Generate once from E: temperature 1.0, 8 samples per prompt, both directions, execution-graded.
- SFT-unfiltered: first 4 samples per prompt, correct or not.
- SFT-RS: up to 4 correct samples per prompt (rejection sampling, after arXiv 2610.04272, which closed Open-MOPD's 5.5-point OPD–SFT gap to 0.5 this way). Prompts with no correct sample drop out and are counted.
- OPD: on-policy distillation from E with the MarinSkyRL MOPD stack.

**Reporting.** For each arm: CruxEval input and output accuracy, the fraction of the E − B gap recovered, GPU-hours, prompts consumed, and GSM8K as the collapse check. Caveat that applies to every arm: training on the test prompts can transfer memorized answers as well as skill; SFT-RS is the most exposed.

**Not in scope.** Weight merging (needs RL-trained experts that share B's init; none exist) and transfer from the older Snowball experts (none beats B under the matched eval).

**Decision log.**
- 2026-10-06: matched eval of B and the existing experts (E6, E17a, E18, SWE, Stage-3) on MATH500/GSM8K; none beats B, so no promotion to teacher.
- 2026-10-07: MATH500 near ceiling for B → CruxEval chosen; MMLU-Pro and GPQA-D measured as fallbacks.
- 2026-10-07: full SFT over LoRA for building E; LoRA kept as the fallback if full SFT collapses out-of-domain.
- 2026-10-07: rejection-sampled SFT added as a third arm.

topics.title: [iris] Quarantine nodes with persistent isolated S3 failures
topics.body:
Add bounded S3 write/read/delete probes to the Kubernetes node agent. Each probe uses the task storage endpoint and credentials and writes a small scratch object per node incarnation. The controller cordons persistent outliers only after a fresh majority of nodes successfully probes the same target after the failure began. Node UID, boot ID, report freshness, environment revision, and Kubernetes resource versions fence stale evidence and concurrent changes.

Group checks under `kubernetes_provider.node_health` with a shared cordon budget. The production `cw-rno2a`, `cw-us-east-02a`, and `cw-us-east-08a` configs probe the shared `marin-us-east-02a` bucket under one-day scratch expiry. The node agent continues probing while cordoned. A fresh success from the current node and configured target after the cordon uncordons a node quarantined by Iris and releases its budget, including after a reboot or credential rotation. Operator cordons remain. Running tasks are not evicted.

Health and cordon evidence remain in node annotations when Finelog is unavailable. Configuration, scratch-object lifecycle, and recovery are documented in the CoreWeave guide. The node-local storage failure that motivated this check is recorded in the [hero incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/599).

To release a cordon, `reconcile_storage_health` must get a healthy report with the same node UID, boot ID, and target as the cordon report ([storage_health.py#L206-L212](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/04b76b9324c8457a31d0db6bd3d5eeb726531d8b/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/node_agent/storage_health.py#L206-L212)). topics.title: [grafana] Prepare GPU history by requested priority
topics.body:
Prepare seven-day H100 and Blackwell (GB200) allocation-history panels grouped by each child job's requested priority. An Interactive request dispatched as Batch stays in the Interactive group. There is no applied-priority lookup or toggle. Iris and Finelog server code, persisted schemas, retention and writes are unchanged.

The projection sums requested GPU sizes over recorded attempt execution intervals at common sampling instants, with cadence chosen from the selected range: one minute through six hours, five minutes through two days, and fifteen minutes through seven days. Exact historical pod binding/cleanup intervals and allocatable capacity remain unavailable. The requested-GPU series therefore recovers only part of allocation; every point is marked incomplete and idle stays blank. Missing regional inputs leave blank spans. Coverage compares Finelog per-root Running task counts with retained attempt intervals, including CPU tasks; differences flag incomplete or inconsistent task history. It also reports setup tasks and unresolved GPU models. Without assignment creation times, the reader cannot establish when setup began, so setup GPU quantities stay blank.

The production metadata reader remains to be implemented and wired; without one the bridge returns HTTP 503. An approved temporary pilot used Grafana's actual CW service identity plus five-minute Iris dashboard-role cookies over the public Kubernetes controller proxy in all three regions. Existing job/resource/full-retry reads succeeded, GetCurrentUser reported dashboard, and SELECT1 was denied by Iris with HTTP 403. All temporary Role/RoleBinding objects were deleted and absence verified; Grafana's original proxy403 returned afterward. No production grants, credentials or deployment remain from the pilot. The minimal tested transport scope is services/proxy on iris/iris-controller-svc:10000; this reader's POST RPCs need the Kubernetes create verb, plus separate read-only Iris authentication.

A straightforward job/task-API reader would require at least 44,398 inventory calls over the captured sampled cohort, before additional pages and full-retry calls. This is a request-count estimate, not measured production latency. Existing controller backups offer a possible bulk alternative without controller changes: recent backups exist in all three regions. One GB200 backup was 25.4 MB compressed and 421.6 MB decompressed; it downloaded in 1.17s, decompressed in 0.22s, and returned 5,712 retained attempts in a 0.032s immutable local SQL query on devbox. Regional coverage, Cloud Run memory/refresh cost, and scoped object-read credentials still need validation before choosing and wiring that reader. Existing backups already contain requested band and current task band; older attempts do not have their own applied-band field.

All 421 Grafana tests and pre-commit checks passed. The requested-only preview uses captured task-state and regional metadata, with 672 common fifteen-minute instants per model. Every point is incomplete; 226 instants show a difference between per-root Running counts and retained intervals. Earlier applied-view replay timings are retained as prior measurements; production requested-reader loading and refresh costs remain unmeasured.

topics.title: Pod creation fails on a node with 65K empty Silo cgroups
topics.body:
On October 2, new pods failed to start on CoreWeave node `g5bc6da`, blocking new jobs. Kubernetes reported `no space left on device` while creating a pod’s cgroup, the kernel group used to track and limit container resources. The node still reported healthy, and its filesystem had 3.55 TB free.

The host cgroup tree had 65,535 descendant groups. Of these, 65,412 were under `/silo`; that entire subtree contained no processes. This strongly suggests exhaustion of the kernel’s roughly 64K memory-cgroup ID space, though we have not traced the failing allocator.

Silo is the nested container runtime running inside our privileged Iris job `muchanem.cap-pipeline-host-53`. Two sampled container IDs from its `containerd-shim` processes matched empty `/silo` cgroups. This points to a cleanup problem in that workload’s runtime, but we have not identified the code path responsible. We have no evidence that CoreWeave’s host containerd created these groups.

Please investigate whether completed containers leave cgroups and shim processes behind, and fix the cleanup path. Verify that repeated container creation and teardown do not keep increasing either count. Coordinate cleanup of the affected node with the pipeline owner; an empty cgroup alone does not establish that it is safe to remove while the runtime is active.

---

topics.title: [grafana] Bound bridge memory during queries and pod scans
topics.body:
Release query inputs when a cached failure is recorded, and allow at most two dashboard computations, with each slot held from source loading through projection. Cached errors preserve their message and HTTP classification without retaining traceback locals or response bodies. Arrow cache accounting includes full referenced buffers.

Stream Kubernetes pod scans one page at a time and query watched deployments directly for the control-plane crashloop alert. Malformed Kubernetes JSON responses produce HTTP upstream failures rather than partial results. Keep Grafana's Cloud Run memory limit at 4 GiB in Pulumi.

The incident exhausted both the previous 2 GiB limit and a 4 GiB replacement. Local reproductions retained 192 MiB through failed queries in a cache capped at 128 MiB; the change releases those tables. A 2,500-pod synthetic scan fell from 108 MiB to 32 MiB peak Python allocations with identical results. These reproductions establish memory defects; they do not identify every contributor to the production OOMs.

[Incident and reproduction details](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/655).

topics.title: [grug] Hide the hero's bare MoE transports behind shared and chunk GEMMs
topics.body:
Under the hero's carry offload, every MoE transport except one ~1 ms routing-weight return now runs beside a GEMM, which shortens the step by 0.73% (12.730 to 12.638 s) and cuts exposed collective time from 1.19 to 0.85 s/step. Before, with one collective in flight, the first forward dispatch and both recomputed dispatches of the backward ran bare (0.63 s/step), and small collectives inside the routed-MoE section held the slot through expert GEMMs. Three changes that only work together fix the schedule:

- The MLP section's FSDP weight all-gathers, the QB router statistics and the drop count complete before the first dispatch. The statistics are saved for the backward, so its recompute does not rerun their all-reduces.
- The routed MoE runs caller work beside its first dispatch (`DispatchOverlap`), and the block hands it the first shared expert's gate/up projections. Barriers order the remaining transports so that each has an expert or chunk GEMM beside it, in the forward and in the backward's recompute.
- Each layer's carry offload copy starts after the layer's weight slices. XLA puts the 4.3 ms carry copy and the slices on the same memcpy streams in program order, and without this ordering the weight prefetch lands a slice behind the copy and stalls the layer (98-152 ms/step on the production wheel). On #9708's head, disabling only this ordering slowed the step by 0.79%.

Configurations without the carry offload keep the plain path. Neither path is safe under XLA's default scheduler, which can start two transports together, so the launcher refuses a ragged carry-offload run whose XLA flags switch the latency-hiding scheduler off. `forward_barrier` is an `optimization_barrier` whose backward passes cotangents straight through, so a weight gradient's all-reduce and FSDP slice still fuse into a reduce-scatter.

In a four-GPU gate, loss and drop counts are bitwise unchanged and gradients change at rounding level, within the difference between two runs of the same code. In the hero the carry ordering also moves fusion boundaries, so its forward changes at rounding level.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

topics.title: [grug] Fuse the expert dSwiGLU and skip recomputed pre-activation stores
topics.body:
Two changes to the routed experts' QuACK kernels, each bitwise or within bf16 rounding:

| Change | Kernel | Hero step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SwiGLU backward and the routing-weight row dot in the dh GEMM's epilogue | 3.54 ms against 5.10 ms per expert chunk | 13.059 to 12.943 s (+0.89%) |
| No gate/up pre-activation store in a forward whose residuals are recomputed | 6.14 ms against 6.48 ms per median chunk, 96 chunks per step | 12.652 to 12.611 s (+0.33%) |

The expert MLP backward wrote dh = dy @ W2^T to HBM and read it back with the gate/up pre-activations in an elementwise pass for the SwiGLU backward and the row dot <h, dh>. A QuACK epilogue on the grouped dh GEMM now unpacks the interleaved (gate, up) tile, applies the SwiGLU backward to the fp32 accumulator, writes the packed (d_gate, d_up) and reduces the row dot, so dh is never materialized. Outputs, drops and dW2 are bitwise unchanged; dx, dW13 and dS change at bf16 rounding (median ~1 ulp), because the SwiGLU backward runs on the unrounded accumulator.

Under the hero's layer remat, the forward's gated GEMM wrote the [C, 2I] pre-activations of every chunk, which the backward recomputes. `_routed_experts` declares `optimize_remat`, so such a forward runs a primal that calls the expert MLP's new `apply`, which returns the output alone, and the gated GEMM gains a launcher that never writes the pre-activations. Each chunk's dispatch still waits on the previous chunk's gate/up output. The forward is bitwise unchanged, and removing the change from all of #9708 slowed the step by 0.47%.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

topics.title: [grug] Run the production hero with a PGLE latency profile
topics.body:
The hero's step is about 1.5-1.9% shorter with a PGLE (profile-guided latency estimation) profile, and production does not use one yet. The hero schedules with one collective in flight, and XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so the scheduler treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under a single GEMM. A profile built from the program's own trace replaces those estimates with measured costs.

All four runs below are on the same 64-GPU rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps); the same code ran 0.8% faster on another rack, so only same-rack comparisons count.

| Program | No profile | Own profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack #9830-#9836 with #9835, plus #9829 | 12.695 s | 12.506 s (+1.51%) |
| The same without #9835 | 12.763 s | 12.522 s (+1.92%) |

With a profile, #9835's hand-placed transport ordering was worth 0.13% (12.506 against 12.522 s), so #9835 was closed and its scheduling left to PGLE. Without a profile it was worth 0.54%, which production gives up until it runs with one.

`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/pgle_profile.py` (#9831) builds a profile from one XProf trace, and the hero README describes the trace, build and rerun loop. Automatic PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE`) cannot profile with one process per GPU. A profile matches instructions by name, so it applies only to the program it was traced from: production needs a profile traced on its own 11-rack mesh, rebuilt after any change to the model, mesh or XLA flags. A stale profile loses the gain without an error.

Done when: the production hero runs with a profile built from its own program, the launcher warns or fails when the profile does not match the compiled program, and the production step-time change is recorded here.

Part of #9636.

comments.body:
🤖 Two ways a profile can break a hero run, both found on one rack while testing the stack (#9830-#9834). A production rollout needs a guard for each.

**1. XLA compile abort (fixed in a candidate plugin, not yet promoted).** With `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading` (#9831), rematerialization may offload values to host when its estimate of the step exceeds its budget. One profiled schedule overshot the budget (124.77 GiB against 114.09 GiB inside the layer loop), and remat picked an f32[] operand of an all-reduce whose start was scheduled before the loop and whose done came after it. `GetCostOfHostOffload` counts users reached through the all-reduce's alias; `OffloadInstruction` places the reload before direct users only, found none unplaced, and failed `CHECK(!place_before_list.empty())` at hlo_rematerialization.cc:2118 on every rank. The bug is unchanged on openxla/xla main and has no upstream report.
- Fix: skip candidates whose buffer `has_indirect_uses` in `GetCostOfHostOffload`, as recomputation already does. Branch `marin/remat-offload-indirect-uses` (0f6dc61dee) on marin-community/xla. A plugin built from it on Iris (`0.11.1+marin.0f6dc61dee6d`, 15 minutes) compiles the case that aborted.
- A second branch, `marin/remat-no-offload-strategy` (ff858b5447), also keeps the flag's host accounting but turns the offload strategy off. Its cost model prices host copies at HBM bandwidth. It is built but untested on the rack.

**2. Out of memory at runtime.** With the fix, the same program compiled and then failed to allocate its 143.75 GiB pool on the first step. Remat estimated the profiled schedule about 26 GiB above the unprofiled one. A near-identical program (the shared expert as two custom VJPs instead of one) trained with its own profile at 119.5 GiB peak, so this depends on the schedule. I have not traced which buffers grow.

What this adds to the done criteria: before a long run, a preflight that compiles the profiled program and runs a few steps, with a fallback to no profile when either fails. Both failures appear within minutes of start.

topics.title: [grug] Add a token-deduplicated ring_dedup expert-parallel MoE backend
topics.body:
Add `ring_dedup`, an opt-in expert-parallel MoE backend selected with `moe_implementation="ring_dedup"`. `ring` all-gathers every token to every expert shard and reduce-scatters a full-size output. With top-4 of 256 experts over 8 shards, a token reaches 3.3 shards on average, so most of those bytes go to shards that do no work on them.

`ring_dedup` sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its top-4 experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`. A small metadata `all_to_all` carries the combine weights and local expert ids, and a trailer row holds the sender's valid count. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule and the Triton `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32, and returns one row per token. Every hidden-width movement is a gather, so neither pass uses a scatter-add. Ring's local assignment selection moves into a helper that both backends call; ring's behavior is unchanged.

The sender capacity per destination is `pooled_transport_capacity_factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing, and `moe_mlp` raises if it is unset. It reuses the `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` parameter so one benchmark flag sets the sender capacity for both backends. The June benchmark sets it with `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` from #9852; 1.1 gave no sender drops. At batch 64 each collective moves 537 MB per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring.

On CPU in f32, the 8-shard tests match ring and a dense reference to 1e-5 in outputs and gradients, including forced sender drops. At full shapes in bf16 the output differs from ring by 0.2-0.5% relative, because `ring_dedup` sums in f32. The drop rate is 1.00-1.12%, against 0.93-0.99% for ring.

June Snowball 67B-A2B, 8x MI350X, EP8, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile caches:

| Remat | ring | ring_dedup | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `save_moe` | 1.730 s (13.07% MFU) | 1.580 s (14.31% MFU) | 454012 / 454021 |
| `recompute_all` | 1.798 s | 1.688 s | 454022 / 454026 |

One `ring_dedup` run (job 454010) ran out of memory on GPU 7 at step 5 and hung; its retry passed. Ring with reference attention also runs out of memory at step 5 at batch 96, and that failure is being diagnosed separately. We have not measured `ring_dedup` on TPU or NVIDIA.

Stacked on #9860, whose gather helpers (`_dispatch_rows`, `_combine_rows` in `ep_ring.py`) this reuses. It does not need the routing top-k from #9889, but the timings above include it. topics.title: [zephyr] Abort ThreadedBatchWriter output when the producer fails
topics.body:
When the body of a ThreadedBatchWriter `with` block raised, `__exit__` sent
the normal end-of-stream sentinel. The write function then completed, and
`write_parquet_file` committed the partial file through `atomic_rename`.
Stages that treat an existing output file as "shard done" then skipped the
shard on a re-run and kept the partial output. The normalize main/dups writer
and the datakit quality writer use this pattern.

`__exit__` now sets an abort event before it wakes the thread. The next read
of the write function's stream raises `WriterAbortedError`, so `atomic_rename`
removes its temporary file and nothing is committed. A normal close is
unchanged.

The datakit quality stage in #9694 removes partial outputs after the fact
(`_discard_outputs`); with this change, that code is not necessary.

topics.title: [grug] Run the shared experts' SwiGLU in QuACK GEMM epilogues
topics.body:
The hero's shared experts run their gate/up and down projections as QuACK GEMMs with SwiGLU and its backward in the epilogues: forward and backward of one shared expert take 13.93 ms instead of 14.51 ms at the hero's per-GPU shape (65536 tokens, width 6144, intermediate width 3072). Removing the change from all of #9708 slows the step by 0.35% and 0.22% in two pairs of runs.

With every PR of this stack and #9829, one 64-GPU hero rack ran 12.590 s/step (31.18% MFU), against 13.899 s (28.24% MFU) for main at #9708's base, with loss within 4.9e-4 of a run of #9708.

Each shared expert runs as two per-shard ops: a gate/up GEMM against interleaved weights with SwiGLU in its epilogue, returning the pre-activations and h, and a down op whose backward runs the SwiGLU backward in the dh GEMM's epilogue. dx and the gate/up weight gradient are single GEMMs on the interleaved layout. The split keeps the gate/up projection movable, so #9835 can run the first shared expert's gate/up beside the first dispatch. The weights stay separate FSDP leaves, gathered inside the shard map, so their gradients still reduce-scatter. Without QuACK, for another activation, or for operands other than bfloat16, the same ops run as XLA einsums.

Since only the down op reads h, the gate/up op stops h's gradient; otherwise the dispatch overlap would hand back dense zeros for h and the backward would run a SwiGLU backward over [T, 2I] per layer that adds nothing. SwiGLU now runs on the fp32 accumulator. Against an fp32 reference in a 4-GPU model gate, the loss error moves from 5.1e-5 to 4.5e-5 and the shared-expert gradient error from 1.22e-2 to 1.15e-2.

Directly on #9835 the change measured -0.11% (12.638 to 12.652 s): there the shared GEMMs cover the transports, and the shorter GEMMs left 0.24 s/step more transport exposed. Measured without #9835 it gained 0.72%, with peak HBM 123.4 to 121.9 GiB.

The QuACK availability check moves to `levanter.grug._moe.availability` and asks the default device for its platform. The shared experts' kernel selection calls it outside the ragged backend, where a test that stubs `jax.default_backend` on CPU devices would make the old check's `jax.devices("gpu")` raise.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

topics.title: [datakit] Register the hero quality data as Datakit steps
topics.body:
Register the hero quality data as two Datakit steps and make the store-ready
dataset a StepSpec output. `bucket.quality_step` reads three co-partitioned leaves
of a source (the normalized shard for row order, the fusion score leaf, and the
content-type leaf), applies the per-type calibration, and writes one shard per
basename with `source`, `id`, `content_type`, `raw_score`, `score` and
`quality_bucket` in the normalized row order. Its artifact is the `QualityScores`
the store already consumes, so `build_clustered_store` reads it unchanged.
`hero_data.quality` resolves that step's identity, and `run.py --stage bucket`
produces it for every registered source.

`score_fusion.fusion_score_step` is the producer of record for the raw scores: one
Zephyr task per normalized shard on GPU workers, tokenizing the text through the
tokenize stage's own core and reading the Harrier embedding by position. The Nemotron
tokenize leaves the August 14 run read were deleted from S3 after it, so the run's
scores are registered by path map as `hero_data.fusion_scores` rather than
rescored; a rerun of the score stage lands at the step's own identity. The
content-type leaves written beside those scores are registered the same way as
`hero_data.content_type`, and `hero_data.harrier` now returns a frozen step so the
score step can depend on it.

Every input leaf of a source holds the normalized shard's documents in its row
order. A census over all 162,535 shards of the 292 sources found every
fusion-score, content-type and Harrier shard in exactly the normalized order, with
the same ids and row counts. Both steps therefore read their side inputs by
position and check each batch's ids against the normalized shard, so a leaf from a
different normalize run fails its shard. `QualityScores.samples_output_dir` is
removed; the stage report reads its spot-check text from the normalized shard of
the same basename.

The model directory moves to `datakit/models/quality/nemotron_88k`, relative to
`MARIN_PREFIX`, with the config fields of the removed bigram, MoE, frozen-donor
and dtype arms dropped from `model.py` and the saved meta. `QualityPin` carries
separate digests for the scorer artifacts and the calibration file, checked by the
worker before it writes, so a refit calibration moves the bucketed dataset without
moving or rescoring the raw scores. Manifest entries for `harrier`, `fusion_scores`,
`content_type` and `quality` cover all 292 sources. The fusion checkpoint's
document-embedding weights form one optional `DocFusion` submodule whose field
order matches the serialized leaves, so the deployed checkpoint loads to identical
weights and scores, and the calibration file parses into a `Calibration`
dataclass.

The bucket stage has run over all 292 sources: 18,710,478,349 documents in
162,535 shards, equal to the fusion-score totals, in 2h50m with 12 sources in
flight on CPU workers. On `nsf_awards` (3 shards, 381,789 documents) the output
reproduced the normalized row order, the pinned raw scores and content types, and
the calibrated buckets on every row. The score stage run from text against the
same embeddings matched the pinned scores to a maximum difference of 1.6e-3 (mean
2.3e-4), the bf16 reduction-order noise of a 4,096-document batch against the
earlier 32,768.

topics.title: [grug] Correct hero remat and collective scheduling; build PGLE profiles
topics.body:
Carry-offloaded hero runs stop recomputing ~10 GiB of backward values per step that already fit in HBM, which shortens the step by 1.04% (13.874 to 13.732 s against #9830 on one 64-GPU hero rack, restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps). Ragged runs without the carry offload run their collectives one at a time, and `pgle_profile` builds an XLA PGLE profile from one trace of the train step. No model code changes.

With the layer carry offloaded to pinned host memory, XLA's `HloRematerialization` charged the 36 GiB carry stack against the device memory limit and recomputed values that fit (143 remat clones, 0.63 s/step of compute). The launcher now defaults `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading=true` whenever the carry is offloaded, so remat counts host buffers as host memory. Only the remat pass reads the flag, after scheduling and copy insertion, so it cannot reorder the carry reload against its consumer. The flag also lets remat offload values to host itself when its estimate of the step exceeds its budget, and that path aborts compilation in XLA's `OffloadInstruction` (hlo_rematerialization.cc:2118) when it picks the operand of a collective still in flight. At memory fraction 0.75 and slop factor 85 the budget is 87.7 GiB and remat estimates the step at 96.8 GiB, so the hero crashed at compile. The carry offload therefore also defaults to 0.78 and 105, a 114 GiB budget, and remat then leaves the step alone ("Rematerialized 0 instructions").

A ragged run without the carry offload keeps the latency-hiding scheduler off, and the collective overlap limit binds only that scheduler, so XLA's default scheduler can start two ragged transports at once. Compiled for a mocked EP64 topology, the program does so in the forward and in the backward, and on GB200 several collectives in flight have hung the ragged transport or given run-to-run different gradients. The launcher now forces `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES` for that configuration.

XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so with one collective in flight it treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under one GEMM. A profile built by `pgle_profile` from the program's own trace shortened the hero step with all of #9708 from 12.611 to 12.515 s (+0.77%). A profile applies only to the program it was traced from, so nothing uses one by default; the README describes the trace, build and rerun loop, and #9879 tracks using one in production.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [grug] Keep AdamH updates finite on zero-norm matrices
topics.body:
scale_by_adamh projects onto the parameter's Frobenius sphere by dividing by
the updated matrix norm. A zero matrix stays zero through a zero learning-rate
or zero-gradient step, so the division is 0/0 and the update is NaN. Floor
that norm at 1e-10, the same floor the direction step already uses.

Fixes #9054

topics.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
topics.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. topics.title: Bound Zephyr shuffle buffers and export execution counters
topics.body:
Bound shuffle input buffers by serialized payload size and row count, so wide records reach the memory-aware writer before accumulating in memory. Stream execution result serialization directly to storage.

Export live and completed coordinator counters to Finelog under the execution ID. Final snapshots are emitted when each execution completes, including dedicated pools and runs shorter than the periodic interval. Counter samples use current-snapshot semantics so completed tasks are not counted twice. Endpoint discovery failures leave telemetry disabled without blocking the coordinator.

topics.title: [grug] Add hero launch controls for a context-length switch
topics.body:
The scaling-ladder launcher takes --seq-len and holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, gate/router weight decay, and run_progress therefore match the 4K run. A changed context requires an explicit --qk-mult, applied to all attention layers; --capacity-factor overrides the expert receiver capacity. A resume at a new context also requires --context-switch-step, which sets the data history the Harrier sources continue from, and --flops-baseline-step/--flops-baseline-total. Hero eval stays at 4K packing.

trigger_hero.sh records the context, batch, QK multiplier, capacity, eval context, FLOPs baseline, and context switch step in the W&B lineage and the #8506 launch record, and checks the FLOPs baseline against the parent run's logged total at the fork row. launch_diagnostics gains --optimizer-tokens-per-step, --gate-router-weight-decay, --eval-seq-len, and --eval-prefix, so a one-rack rehearsal can use the hero's optimizer settings and report long-context eval under a separate prefix. Diagnostics with --eval-every now score the uncheatable sets as well as Paloma.

The live run is unchanged: trigger_hero.sh still launches at 4K. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

topics.title: [levanter] Continue mixture reads across a context-length switch
topics.body:
Harrier now shuffles blocks of 2^20 tokens (io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len). At 4K this is the existing 256-sequence block, so the live run's data order is unchanged. At a longer context the outer block permutation stays the same, and only the order of sequences inside each 512-block shuffle window changes. With sequence-sized blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T.

LmDataConfig.prior_phases describes the earlier context lengths of a resumed run. Each source then skips the unread rest of the shuffle window it was reading at the switch step and starts its next window, so nothing is served twice. At a 216000-step handoff this skips about 52B tokens, 0.65% of the rest of the run. MixtureDataset takes per-source start offsets to apply the skip. Every phase must give positive weight to the same sources, because a training config drops zero-weight sources and that changes the shuffle keys of the rest; a change in the active sources is rejected. The offsets come from each source's true position in the earlier phase, so they also absorb the main-mixture boundary moving from step 108000 to 108096 at 16K. The grug train loop builds its mixture through the new LmDataConfig.train_mixture.

topics.title: [grug] Select the hero router's top-k experts with a Triton kernel
topics.body:
The hero router's top-(K+1) expert selection runs in a Triton kernel instead of a full XLA sort of every row: 0.096 ms per call instead of 0.856 ms at [65536, 384], k = 9 on one GB200, once in the forward and again in the recompute. The indices and their order match `jax.lax.top_k` bitwise for every input, including ties, signed zeros, infinities and NaNs.

XLA:GPU uses its own top-k kernel only for rows of at least 1,024 elements, so 384-expert rows fall back to a sort. The new kernel takes float32 rows narrower than 1,024 on a GPU device; everything else keeps `jax.lax.top_k`. Its gate asks the default device whether it is a GPU, because a hero test stubs `jax.default_backend` to trace a GPU-only path on CPU devices. The Triton gather-sum's gate makes the same check.

One warp holds one row in registers, as one power-of-two tile or, when that pads less, three equal ones (a 384-wide row is three 128-wide tiles), and takes k successive maxima over XLA's float32 total-order key, breaking ties by the lower column. A row in one warp keeps both reductions inside the warp; Triton reduces across warps through shared memory. A taken or absent entry gets the smallest key and the column n, which the lowest-column reduction never returns, so a negative NaN with payload 0xFFFFFFFF, whose key is also the smallest, is not mistaken for one. The kernel reads an int32 view of the input, so autodiff never asks it for a JVP rule. For k above 16 the steps run in a loop, which compiles in 0.2 s where unrolled steps take 36 s at k = 384.

No rack run measured this kernel alone. On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), an earlier version that took 0.125 ms per call shortened the step by 0.53%.
